title: Temporary token embedded in a client-side upload script
summary: A browser script that uploads data to Mapbox holds a temporary token (header tk) that the application obtained from the Tokens API for that one upload workload.
rationale: The provider tells client applications to use a temporary token for sensitive operations such as uploads, and also says tokens with secret scopes must not be exposed to the client. A temporary token has the same three-part shape as the public and secret tokens, carries the scopes of its workload and expires within one hour. The documentation does not say whether such a token in client code is exposed secret material, so the situation is an open question, not an instance of a rule that applies to every family.

expectation.rationale: Not assertable. The provider's statements point in different directions: client applications should use temporary tokens for sensitive operations, yet tokens with secret scopes must not be exposed to the client, and a temporary token expires within one hour. Candidate outcomes for a maintainer to decide, as a recorded project-policy decision with a non-author reviewer: must be flagged (it carries secret scopes while it is live), may be flagged (it is short-lived by design), must not be flagged (the provider intends it in clients). A statement from Mapbox on whether a temporary token in client code counts as an exposed credential would settle it as provider-documented. No fixture exists, so nothing is asserted.

sources.supports: If you need to do potentially sensitive operations in the client (for example, uploading new data or deleting styles) use the Tokens API to generate a temporary token for the specific workload; a client application should only use a token with public scopes.
Do not expose access tokens with secret scopes; make all requests requiring a token with secret scopes on a server.
When creating a temporary token, the expiration must be no more than one hour in the future.
